$comment: The repository settings that are NOT code — branch rules and merge policy — written down because nothing else can hold them. A clone carries every gate in this tree, and none of these: delete the repository and they are gone, recreate it and they come back as GitHub's defaults, which are not these. That is the failure this file exists to prevent, and it is not hypothetical — `ci-gate` being a required check is the only thing standing between a red run and a merge. Apply with `gh api --method PUT repos/ecoma-io/ecoma --input <the repository object>` and `gh api --method POST repos/ecoma-io/ecoma/rulesets --input <a rulesets entry>`; read the live state back with the same paths and `GET` to diff it against this file. This is a record, not an enforcer: no gate compares it to reality, because doing so needs an admin token and this repository holds none. Check it by hand when something about landing a change feels different from what is written here. One reader does compare it and publishes the answer, though: OpenSSF Scorecard's `Branch-Protection` check, run from `.github/workflows/scorecard.yml`, reads this ruleset over the public GraphQL API — rulesets are readable without an admin token where classic branch protection is not, so the published score is a live audit of the rules below and no maintainer PAT is involved in producing it. Each rule below records which of that check's tiers it satisfies; the tier definitions are the pinned Scorecard release's own `docs/checks.md#branch-protection`, not a restatement kept here.

repository.$comment: Merge policy. Exactly one method stays enabled, so the strategy is a mechanism rather than whichever button someone clicked. `delete_branch_on_merge` is safe under merge commits and only under them: a merge commit's second parent puts the branch's commits on the default branch as the SAME objects, so deleting the ref removes a pointer and no history. Under rebase the branch commits are REPLAYED as new objects and the originals are reachable only through that ref — which is why 88 stale branches had accumulated before this file existed.

rules.$comment: Tier 1 of Scorecard's `Branch-Protection` check, one of its two halves — `non_fast_forward` below is the other. That tier is a gate, not a bucket: the check awards nothing at any higher tier until BOTH are present, so a repository already satisfying Tier 3 publishes a 0 while either is missing. This costs nothing in practice — the default branch is never deleted in ordinary work, and a repository reset that genuinely needs the rule gone drops it deliberately rather than by accident.

Tier 1's other half. Blocks force-push to the default branch, which rewrites landed history and silently invalidates every commit pinned off it — the merge queue's would-be-trunk runs, and the git reference the private control-plane workspace consumes this harness at.

`required_linear_history` is deliberately ABSENT. It forbids merge commits outright — a `PUT .../pulls/N/merge` with `merge_method: merge` answers `405 Merge commits are not allowed on this repository` even while the repository object says they are. Linearity is recoverable as a view (`git log --first-parent`, `git bisect --first-parent`); the pull-request boundary a merge commit records is not recoverable at all once a rebase has flattened it, and that boundary is what makes `git revert -m 1 <merge>` the one operation the engineering charter §2 promises. Scorecard's `Branch-Protection` tiers land almost entirely on this rule's parameters, and three of them sit below the maximum on purpose. `require_code_owner_review: true` satisfies half of Tier 4; the other half is a code owners file, which `.github/CODEOWNERS` provides, so that half already passes. `required_approving_review_count: 0` forfeits Tier 2 and the rest of Tier 4. `require_last_push_approval: false` forfeits one of Tier 2's four requirements. `dismiss_stale_reviews_on_push: false` forfeits half of Tier 5. Those three move together or not at all, and only with a second maintainer: raising either boolean alone buys exactly zero points, because the tier holding it stays gated behind the approval count, and GitHub describes last-push approval as an approval from someone other than the person who pushed — which a solo maintainer cannot supply whatever the count says. `notAppliedYet.reviewApprovalNeedsASecondHuman` carries the arithmetic and the cost.

`integration_id` 15368 is GitHub Actions: it pins the check to the app that produces it, so a differently-owned check of the same name cannot satisfy it. `ci-gate` is a single aggregating job on purpose — one name to require, so adding a CI job never means remembering to add it here too. This rule pays Scorecard's `Branch-Protection` check twice, and both already pass: a non-empty `required_status_checks` list is Tier 3 in full, and `strict_required_status_checks_policy: true` is one of Tier 2's four requirements — the check reads both straight out of this ruleset.

The merge queue the engineering charter §2 states: an approved pull request does not merge directly, it queues and CI re-runs on the would-be trunk — trunk plus the entries ahead of it. `ALLGREEN` is what makes that real rather than decorative: a batch lands only if every entry in it passes together, so the interference case §2 names (two individually-correct changes that are wrong combined) fails the batch instead of landing. `merge_method: MERGE` matches the pull_request rule above; a queue configured to squash or rebase would quietly undo the decision recorded there. THIS RULE HAS A CODE DEPENDENCY, and it is the one place in this file where enabling a setting alone makes things worse than leaving it off: the queue waits for `ci-gate` to report on the temporary queue ref, so `.github/workflows/ci.yml` must list `merge_group` among its triggers. Without it nothing runs there, no check reports, and every entry waits out `check_response_timeout_minutes` and is dropped — a queue that accepts pull requests and merges none, with no error anywhere saying so. Removing that trigger and keeping this rule is the failure mode; they change together or not at all.

notAppliedYet.$comment: Two kinds of entry, both about the distance between this file and the live repository, so a reader can tell a record from a wish. Most are gaps waiting on rights: everything applied here needs an admin token, and the sessions that maintain this file hold a fine-grained token without one — they can READ the ruleset but not write it. The last is the opposite case, a setting this file deliberately does NOT target, recorded so its absence reads as a decision rather than an oversight; the `rulesets` block above stays applyable exactly as written, and nothing in this block is part of it. Re-check with `gh api repos/ecoma-io/ecoma/rulesets/{id}` — a stale entry here is worse than none, because it reads as a known gap when it is really an unread one.
notAppliedYet.deletionAndNonFastForward: Live: BOTH ABSENT, re-verified against `GET /repos/ecoma-io/ecoma/rulesets/{id}`. Target: both present, as recorded above. Without `deletion` the default branch can be deleted outright; without `non_fast_forward` it can be force-pushed, which rewrites landed history and silently invalidates every commit pinned off it — the merge queue's would-be-trunk runs, and the git reference the private control-plane workspace consumes this harness at. They were live before the merge-method change and are not now. This is now also the single reason the published Scorecard `Branch-Protection` score is 0 rather than 4: those two rules are that check's Tier 1, Tier 1 gates every tier above it, and every requirement this repository already meets — pull requests required, a status check required, that check strict, code owner review required — scores nothing while either is missing. Closing this gap needs no other change and no second person. If dropping them was deliberate — a repository reset needs `deletion` gone to proceed — then restoring them belongs on the checklist for the tree that replaces this one, because nothing here will notice their absence.
notAppliedYet.claAppBypassAndSecrets: DECIDED, and the CLA flow stays inert until the four steps below are done — `.github/workflows/cla.yml` asks whether the App exists in a `credentials` job and SKIPS its `cla` job rather than half-working. Skipped and not failed, deliberately: `cla` is not one of the required checks recorded above (`ci-gate` is the only one), so a red X for an unset secret blocked no merge and gated no contribution while appearing on every pull request — and a check that is always red is a check nobody reads on the day it means something. A green one would be worse, claiming a CLA was checked when none was. The named reason moved to a workflow warning, and the check becomes real the moment step 4 lands, with no further code change. The problem it answers: recording a signature means committing to the default branch, the `pull_request` rule above requires a pull request for every such change, and the fix everyone reaches for first DOES NOT EXIST — `github-actions[bot]` cannot be put on a bypass list at all. It is not selectable in the ruleset UI and no integration id is accepted for it over the API, because GitHub keeps its own Actions token non-bypassable on purpose: write access to a workflow file must never become write access past every rule. A bypass list takes repository roles, teams, GitHub Apps and deploy keys. So the write is made by the organisation's own GitHub App, which IS eligible. The rejected alternative, for the record: point the action's `branch:` input at a branch this ruleset does not cover (its condition is `~DEFAULT_BRANCH` only, so every other branch is already unprotected and no settings change would be needed) — cheaper, but it moves the signature off the branch CI checks out, and keeping the signature where an ordinary clone already has it was judged worth the setup. THE FOUR STEPS, all needing rights this session does not hold: (1) the App must be installed on this repository with `contents: write` (the signature commit), `pull-requests: write` (the comment), `statuses: write` (the check) and `actions: write` (the re-run on `recheck`) — the workflow's own `permissions:` block is `contents: read` and deliberately cannot substitute for any of them; (2) add the App to this ruleset's `bypass_actors` as `{ actor_id: <the App's id>, actor_type: "Integration", bypass_mode: "always" }`; (3) generate a private key for the App; (4) store its id and that key as the repository secrets `CLA_APP_ID` and `CLA_APP_PRIVATE_KEY`, whose names the workflow reads and this file does not duplicate anywhere else. Step 2 is the one silently skipped: the token mints fine without it and the commit is refused, so verify the bypass entry exists rather than inferring it from a green token step. STEP 2 ALSO COSTS A SCORECARD POINT, and the cost is worth stating before it is paid rather than discovered: `Branch-Protection` derives 'protection applies to administrators' from the bypass list being EMPTY — any actor on any ruleset matching the default branch, admin or not, flips it to false. That is half of Tier 5, so a repository otherwise at 10 lands at 9 the moment the App is added. The trade is deliberate and the App still wins: an inert CLA flow is a worse outcome than a nine, and the alternative that keeps the bypass list empty moves the signature off the branch CI checks out, which was already rejected above.
notAppliedYet.reviewApprovalNeedsASecondHuman: NOT a gap and NOT a target — the one entry here recording something this file deliberately leaves unset, because the reason is a person rather than a permission. Live and target both say `required_approving_review_count: 0`. Raising it is the whole remaining distance in Scorecard's `Branch-Protection` check, and it cannot be paid with configuration. The ladder, derived from the pinned Scorecard release's own tier arithmetic rather than estimated: today 0; adding `deletion` and `non_fast_forward` alone reaches 4 (Tier 1 in full, plus partial credit for the two Tier 2 requirements already met); adding `required_approving_review_count: 1` together with `require_last_push_approval: true` completes Tier 2 and Tier 3 and reaches 8; raising the count to 2 completes Tier 4 and reaches 9; adding `dismiss_stale_reviews_on_push: true` completes Tier 5 and reaches 10, provided the bypass list is still empty. THE COST, in the same breath: GitHub does not let an author approve their own pull request, and `.github/CODEOWNERS` names one person. At a count of 1 the sole maintainer can no longer merge their own work at all; at 2 nobody can merge until a second and third reviewer exist. So the last 6 points are not a settings change, they are a staffing precondition, and the honest reading is that this repository buys 4 of them now and the remaining 6 when it has the people. The same precondition is why the `Code-Review` check also publishes a 0 — one decision moves both.
